context_heading: What to understand when choosing an EIS advisor
context: Tax adviser is not a protected title in the UK, so anyone can call themselves one. The main specialist bodies are the Chartered Institute of Taxation (for the CTA qualification) and the Association of Taxation Technicians (ATT), and their members follow a shared code of professional conduct. Many accountants and solicitors also advise on tax, so it is worth asking about qualifications and experience.

Tax advisers who charge a fee must be supervised for anti-money-laundering purposes, and HMRC has been tightening standards for paid tax agents. Before you go ahead, ask about professional indemnity insurance and how the adviser keeps up to date with EIS rules. When searching for the best EIS advisor near you, compare several advisers on their relevant experience and the questions they ask you.

questions: What experience do you have with EIS advance assurance applications and with companies in my sector?
Are you a member of the Chartered Institute of Taxation or the Association of Taxation Technicians, or do you hold another relevant qualification?

faqs.q: What does an EIS advisor do?
faqs.a: An EIS advisor helps companies get advance assurance from HMRC and comply with Enterprise Investment Scheme rules, and helps investors understand the reliefs and risks. They can guide you through the strict qualifying trade rules and the ongoing requirements of the scheme.

faqs.q: How do I judge who is the best EIS advisor for me?
faqs.a: There is no official ranking of EIS advisers, so the best one for you depends on your circumstances. Ask about their relevant experience, qualifications, how they charge, and whether they can explain the risks as clearly as the reliefs. A good adviser will ask you detailed questions about your plans before quoting.

Tax adviser is not a protected title in the UK, but advisers who charge a fee must be supervised for anti-money-laundering purposes. Many belong to the Chartered Institute of Taxation or the Association of Taxation Technicians, whose members follow a shared code of professional conduct. It is reasonable to ask about qualifications, supervision and professional indemnity insurance.

extra_heading: Getting ready for a first conversation with an EIS adviser
extra: Searching for the best EIS advisor near me often means you want someone you can sit down with, so it is worth thinking about what you will bring to that first meeting. Gather your company's latest accounts, a short description of what the business does and how it earns money, and any notes on the investment you are planning. If you are an investor, bring the details of the opportunity you are considering, including the company's trade and stage.

The first appointment is usually a two-way assessment rather than a sales pitch. A careful adviser will want to test the trade against the strict EIS qualifying rules, ask about your plans for the money and explain where the risks sit for investors. You should leave with a clearer view of whether advance assurance is realistic and what the adviser would need from you to take things further.

Because quotes are on application, ask early how the adviser structures their work and what the quote will cover, so you can compare like with like. Local convenience matters, but so does relevant EIS experience, so weigh both rather than assuming the nearest adviser is the right one for your situation.

extra_faqs.q: Should I choose an EIS adviser who is local to me?
extra_faqs.a: Being nearby can make meetings easier, but it is not the main test. Ask about their experience with EIS advance assurance, their qualifications and how they charge, and let that guide you as much as distance.

extra_faqs.q: What if my company's trade might not qualify under EIS?
extra_faqs.a: The rules on qualifying trades are strict, so raise this at the first conversation. An adviser can talk you through how the rules apply to what your company actually does before you spend time on an advance assurance application.
